runs.text: as obras de peßoa honrada. S.

lines.note: Completes boas obras from f214: good deeds received from an honored person. The repeated as at f214's foot is only a catchword. S. remains an italic usage label.

Hōsen, defensive fighting, is glossed fusegi tatakō. Reſistir corrects the missing i in Reſstir; enlargement shows the i before the short-s/t combination, and the Portuguese verb agrees with resisting an attack.
Hōsen suru supplies the verbal form; the cross-reference begins Co-. Vt and Vide are italic editorial Latin, while the Japanese example is roman.
Completes coxen fǒxen, a paired expression for attack and defense. The accent is worn, so retain the caron consistent with the preceding repeated word rather than inventing a new spelling.
Hōseki, glossed nori no niwa, is a hall or temple for doctrinal preaching. Tera is italic in Portuguese; on continues into onde without adding an unseen hyphen.
Onde ſe prèga da lei completes the preaching-place definition. Preserve the old accent and construction rather than silently changing them to modern Portuguese.

Hōseki here is textile work, glossed umi, tçugumu. The printed tçugumu is retained despite modern tsumugu being more familiar; NINJAL identifies the separate headword, and the Portuguese spinning sense establishes its meaning.
Torcer linho adds twisting linen or flax to spinning. This confirms that the second hōseki is a textile term, not the preceding religious hall.
Hoshi means a star, exactly matched by Eſtrela. The Japanese x represents the sh sound, not Portuguese x semantics.
Hōshi is a tonsured Buddhist cleric. The first Bõzo is visibly roman while the surrounding Portuguese is italic; preserve that local contrast instead of making all occurrences uniform.
Hōshi ni naru means becoming a cleric. The second Bõzo is italic here, illustrating why lexical identity alone cannot determine typeface.

runs.text: Sinal preto q̃ ſe poem no meo do aluo.

lines.note: Hoshi also names the black aiming mark at the center of a target. Read Sinal preto, not Sina lpreto; the l belongs to sinal even with the loose printed spacing.
Mato no hoshi wo nerō means aiming at the target's black center. The Japanese example and Apontar ao preto agree; preserve the caron in the historical contracted verb form.
Do aluo completes the target definition. The physical pre-/to split belongs wholly to Portuguese.

A separate hōshi means gracious intention or goodwill, glossed kōbaxii kokorozaxi. The middle of cocorozaxi is faint, but the surviving letters and the Portuguese goodwill definition support the retained reading.
Go-hōshi ni azzucaru is receiving someone's gracious kindness. The honorific go- and the verb azukaru fit the respectful usage explained below.

runs.text: Receber amizade, ou boa obra dalguem, fa-

lines.note: Receber amizade, ou boa obra explains receiving friendship or a good deed. Dalguem is retained without adding a nasal mark not clearly printed.
Falando com reſpeito marks respectful speech. It is a usage qualification of the Japanese phrase, not an additional literal meaning of hōshi.
Hoshi, ſu, oita is 'dry in the sun'. Oita is the dictionary's historical s-verb past pattern, not an error to modernize to shita.
The metaphorical phrases hara wo hosu and nodo wo hosu mean going without food or drink. Restore the visible initial ¶; the printed foſu contains long ſ even though the headword ends in xi.

runs.text: Estar enxuto ſem ter comido nada,

lines.note: Nodo wo hosu continues across the physical row boundary. Estar enxuto sem ter comido nada explains the metaphor of being dry or empty without eating.
Nem bebido adds lack of drink. This completes the parallel belly/throat expressions without creating a new entry.

runs.text: Parte no ceo onde ſe encontrão

lines.note: Hoshiai no sora is the region of the sky where stars meet. The phrase suggests the star-meeting imagery rather than an ordinary generic sky; retain the dictionary's definition without supplying unstated names.
As estrelas closes that description. The printed short s at the end and the st combination are preserved from OCR rather than normalized on visual preference alone.
Hoshikatame, uru, eta means hardening by drying. The compound hoshi + katame and Secando endurecer support one another.
Hoshikoroshi, ſu, oita means killing through deprivation. The historical oita ending is legitimate here as in hosu above, not to be replaced with a modern past ending.
À ſede adds thirst to starvation. Both parts belong to the definition of hoshikorosu.
Hoshihoshi is equated with mame, beans, as a women's term. The Portuguese reads feijoẽs with a visible i after e, not fejoẽs; retain the nasal mark over e as printed.
Palavra de molheres completes the women's-language label. Molheres is a historical spelling retained from the scan.
Hoshihoshito refers the reader to hoshimeku below. The adverb will describe the texture or sound of undercooked rice, not the beans sense simply because it shares letters.

runs.text: Couſa deſejauel, ou deſejar algũa couſa.

lines.note: Hoshii is 'desirable' or 'to desire'. Read Couſa deſejauel, ou deſejar: the OCR lost or confused u and j, and the recovered Portuguese agrees exactly with the Japanese adjective.
Hoshisa is the nominal derivative, desire or desirability. It is printed on its own indented physical row under hoshii, not a repeated full definition.
Hoshū is the adverbial form of hoshii. The small caron over u is retained, and the row remains separate rather than being collapsed into the previous line.
Foxijmamani resolves to hoshii-mama-ni, 'as one wishes', rather than an unfamiliar single stem. The Portuguese definition agrees with that segmentation; Adu. is italic as printed.
Conforme ao deſejo, ou vontade means according to one's desire or will. It confirms the hoshii-mama-ni construction of the previous row.
Hoshimekaxi, ſu, aita means setting a dog on someone. Açular o cão supplies the meaning; X. is wholly roman, including its full stop.
The Kami-region alternative is qexicaquru, keshikakuru. Cami remains italic inside Portuguese, while the cited Japanese verb and following Inu- are roman.
Inu wo hoshimekasu completes the example of inciting a dog. The long ſ in the verb is retained rather than changed to f by its visual resemblance.
Hoshimenuki is a small iron fitting inserted into a sword assembly. The following line, not the headword alone, specifies the handle and blade and controls the technical interpretation.

runs.text: pellos punhos, & ferro da Catana pera os

lines.note: Read pellos punhos, & ferro da Catana: through the handles and iron of the sword. The OCR's panbos, ferto, and Catara obscure an otherwise coherent description; the scan supports each correction. Catana stays italic here.
Ter mão means holding the pieces secure. This short row completes the explanation of the sword fitting rather than naming a hand as a separate object.
Hoshimeki, u, eita describes rice sounding or feeling hard between the teeth. The paradigm is retained as abbreviated in print; the Portuguese Soar is appropriate for this sensory description.
The rice feels insufficiently cooked inside. Read ſentirſe, restoring the visible r omitted by OCR; Me- begins meshi in the example.
Meshi ga hoshimeku, or hoshihoshito suru, describes that undercooked-rice sensation. This resolves the earlier cross-reference and supports both Japanese expressions.
Hōshi-musha is a tonsured soldier, directly glossed Soldado rapado. The circumflex over o is visible.

runs.text: Beneficio, ou boa obra que ſe faz a al-

lines.note: Hōshin denotes a benefit or good deed. A dark mark outside the left rule was mistaken for ¶; it is not a body pilcrow and is omitted from the text.
Go-hōshin ni azzucaru means receiving this favor. The initial is G and the o has a worn caron, not the OCR's unaccented Cofoxinni; the Portuguese translation continues in column 2.

runs.text: ceber eſte beneficio, ou obra de amor. S.

lines.note: Receber eſte beneficio, ou obra de amor completes the favor example. S. remains italic as printed, and the crop is aligned with this row rather than the header.

runs.text: Fôxin. Fotoqeni ſanjinno tocu arito yǔ,

lines.note: Hōshin, 報身, is defined in Japanese: the Buddha is said to have the virtues of three bodies. This is Japanese explanatory prose, not Portuguese, so Fotoqe ni and sanjinno must stay roman with a kana hint.
It is the second name in that three-body scheme. Hōshin no nyorai follows as an example; Vt alone is italic editorial Latin.
Rai completes nyorai, 如来. Bup. is the roman Buddhist-vocabulary label and not another Japanese syllable to convert.
Hoshina is dried greens or turnips, glossed Nabos ſecos. The Portuguese narrows the dictionary's sense; no modern botanical identification is inserted.
Hoshitsuke, uru, eta means drying in the sun. Enxu continues as enxugar without a visible hyphen, which is deliberately not supplied.

runs.text: gar couſas tintas de cores pera milhor ſe còra-

lines.note: The things dried are dyed, to improve their color. Milhor and còra- preserve the source's Portuguese spelling and accent.

runs.text: rem, ou tomarem milhor cor. ¶ Permet.

lines.note: Tomarem milhor cor closes the literal sense; Permet. introduces the metaphorical use. The printed pilcrow separates senses, not necessarily independent headwords.
Hito wo hoshitsukuru, or hoshitsukete oku, means keeping someone in deprivation. Read foxitçuqete, not foxitçuoete: the q descender and the Japanese conjugation agree.

runs.text: Opprimir a alguẽ com fome, & ſede.

lines.note: The oppression is specifically with hunger and thirst. Qu completes vo-/qu, oku; it is Japanese text, while Opprimir begins the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Certo arroz ſeco muito miudo como cuſcuz.

lines.note: Hoshii is finely divided dried rice, compared with couscous. The final iy belongs to the rice word rather than being silently harmonized with the adjective Foxij above.

runs.text: Eſcrito, ou patente que vem dalgũ of-

lines.note: Fôxe denotes a written order or patent from an official. Its position and meaning suggest hōsho, but the source visibly has e and NINJAL also records Fôxe; retain the printed headword rather than emending it to Fôxo.

runs.text: ficial, ou gouernador por mandado, & ordem

lines.note: The document comes from an official or governor by command and order. Keep the doubled f across of-/ficial and the printed gouernador spelling.
Do ſenhor identifies the lord whose command authorizes the document. The short row completes the preceding administrative definition.
Hōshu is a precious stone or jewel. The accent is faint but the retained caron agrees with NINJAL; no change to the source word is justified merely by its wear.

Hossengio denotes a place for doctrinal debate, glossed hōran no tokoro. NINJAL gives Foxxengiǒ, but enlargement does not establish a surviving accent over the final o here; retain unaccented Foxxengio and record the lexical discrepancy rather than silently adding a mark.
Onde ſe diſputa das leis explains the debating place. Leis here is doctrinal law, as indicated by the Japanese Buddhist context, not necessarily civil legislation.
Hosshi, suru, ita means strongly desiring. The printed ending is ſuru, not ſunu; its r agrees with the irregular Japanese suru paradigm.
A second sense is considering or supposing something to oneself. Cuidar and ter pera ſi should not be forced into the first desire sense.
Hosshin, 法身, is exemplified by hosshin no nyorai. The following Japanese sentence places it first among the Buddha's three bodies, contrasting with hōshin above.
Sanjin to yū ichiban no na means the first name among the three bodies. Bup. is entirely roman, including the stop; remove the OCR's partial italic stop.
Hosshin, 発心, is glossed kokoro wo okosu, arousing the heart or intention. Deuação is the printed form for devotion; it is not normalized to modern devoção.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Com deſejo da ſaluação deixar o

lines.note: The further sense is leaving worldly life with a desire for salvation. The saved OCR detector omitted this row, so its crop was placed manually between the two verified neighboring lines and then read directly.
Hosshin xerareta is a respectful expression for having taken religious vows. Xerareta is the source's se-series spelling, not automatically an OCR error because modern Japanese uses se.

runs.text: do homem que ſe rapou, & deixou o mundo.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly describes a man who shaved his head and left the world. This corroborates the religious reading rather than a generic awakening alone.
Hosshinja is someone desiring salvation. Preserve deſe as printed despite a modern preference for separate words; the expression continues with renunciation below.
Deſprezador do mundo adds one who rejects worldly life. This is the missionary gloss's wording, not an independent judgment added by the reviewer.
Hosshō, 法性, is labeled Buddhist vocabulary and defined as first principle or nature. Bup. is roman; the caron in the Japanese headword is retained.
Natureza do Fotoque completes the reference to Buddha-nature. Fotoque is italic inside Portuguese, despite the roman Japanese prose in the earlier three-body entries.
Hoya names a round red marine creature, called peixe in the source. Do not replace that historical broad description with a modern taxonomic category in Level 1.
Hoyaku is a replenishing remedy, glossed oguinō kusuri. The f in the headword is the historical Japanese h sound; the remedy's action is described below.

runs.text: deſpondo pouco a pouco como enxaropes.

lines.note: The medicine acts gradually, like syrups. Deſpondo and enxaropes are retained source forms rather than modernized spelling.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Mezinha que refaz, ou dà alẽto.

lines.note: Another explanation is a remedy that restores or gives strength. Read dà alẽto, not dàt alẽto: enlargement shows staining through the baseline, not an extra t after dà.
Hōyaku is foolishness or stupidity, a distinct entry from the remedy above. The visible circumflex is important to the source's distinction.

runs.text: Ajuntamento de Bõzos pera algum of-

lines.note: Hōe is an assembly of Buddhist monks for a service. Bõzos remains italic within Portuguese; the stain below does not change the clear first-row wording.

runs.text: ficio, ou cerimonias, ou os meſmos officios, &

lines.note: The term also denotes the ceremonies or services themselves. Os before meſmos is partly obscured by a stain; os is the contextual reading supported by masculine officios, not a claim that both letters are fully visible.
Solennidade finishes the ceremonial sense. The source's doubled n and long ſ are retained.
A separate hōe, 法衣, is glossed nori no koromo, religious clothing. Vestido particular introduces the special garment, with the Portuguese st form preserved.

runs.text: dos Bõzos com que ſe diſtinguẽ dos ſeculares,

lines.note: The monks' garment distinguishes them from laypeople. A comma, not the OCR full stop, ends ſeculares and connects the alternative purpose in the next row.

runs.text: ou com que fazem ſuas ceremonias.

lines.note: The garment is also used for their ceremonies. The relative phrase continues the same clothing definition rather than beginning another entry.
Hōe is equated with yena, ena, the membrane enclosing a fetus. This is distinct from religious hōe; the caron and the native gloss are retained.

runs.text: com que a criança eſtà enuolta no ventre da

lines.note: The child is enclosed in that membrane in the mother's womb. Criança and eſtà are source spellings and accents, not modernized.
Mãy completes 'mother'; i, Parias supplies a Portuguese explanatory synonym for the afterbirth. The whole row is italic, including y, which is not a Japanese one-letter word or kana candidate.
Hoye, uru, eta means barking or bellowing. The source lists a dog and an ox, so the broad Japanese vocalization sense is clear.

runs.text: vyuar lobo, &c. ¶ Item, Per met. Chorar

lines.note: The list adds a wolf's howl and then a metaphorical sense. Vyu ar as spaced by the font is the historical uivar form; retain vyuar rather than modernizing it.

runs.text: de meninos, ou moços falando baixamente.

lines.note: The metaphorical use is crying by children or young people, marked as low-register speech. Falando baixamente is a usage qualification, not necessarily a quiet volume instruction.
Hoye-kakari means springing at someone while barking or howling. The ending is atta, not acta: enlargement resolves the two t characters, supported by kakaru's past form and NINJAL.
Saltar ſobre alguẽ completes the attack definition. Foye at the far right is separately recorded as the page's catchword, not part of this physical body text.
